summary: Defines a media feature tag whose value is a MIME content type. This lets a feature expression say which types of content a device or message can handle.

plainLanguage.summary: A tag lets a device say what kinds of files it can open. This defines one tag that just names the file type.

subtitle: A media feature tag called type that lets a capability expression say which MIME content types it covers.

tldr.problem: Media feature expressions could describe things like color or paper size, but they had no way to name the MIME content type that those details applied to.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2913 defines a feature tag named type whose value is a lower-case MIME type/subtype string with no parameters, so it can sit inside an expression next to other tags.
tldr.outcome: Expressions can now say, for example, that a device handles image/tiff at one set of capabilities and text/plain at another. Parameters such as charset get their own separate tags.

today: RFC 2913 is a Proposed Standard from September 2000. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2913 builds on two earlier documents: RFC 2533, which defines an expression format for describing media feature capabilities, and RFC 2506, which defines how simple media feature tags are registered. A media feature is information about facilities assumed to be available for message content to be rendered or presented. It is not meant to cover information that affects message transmission.

This memo adds one new tag whose value is a MIME content type. That lets a feature expression take account of the content type of the data it describes. The memo uses ABNF from RFC 2234.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a way to write down what a device can show. This memo adds one more word to that way of writing: the kind of file.

sections.title: Why Content Type Belongs in the Expression
sections.content:
The expression syntax was designed to add detail on top of basic MIME content type information. The RFC gives three situations where it helps to put the content type inside the expression itself.

  • Media feature details may depend on the content type. The combining algebra and syntax cannot apply to content type information unless it appears in the expression. In HTTP 1.1 with Transparent Content Negotiation, acceptable types and other features travel in different request headers, with no clear way to say they are acceptable only in certain combinations.
  • Sometimes all capability information should be in a single expression. The DSN and MDN extensions of RFC 2530 offer a single field for it.
  • When features describe message content, they may refer to inner parts of a MIME composite, such as the parts of a multipart, files in a compressed archive, or encrypted data.
sections.plainLanguage: If you say 'I can show color' without saying which kind of file, it is unclear what you mean. Putting the file kind in the same sentence fixes that.

sections.title: The type Feature Tag
sections.content:
The tag is named type and its legal value is a string containing a MIME content-type value, the kind that appears in a Content-type: header. The string must have the form type/subtype, as defined by MIME (RFC 2045), and only lower-case letters should be used.

The content type must be given without any parameters. If information normally carried in a content-type parameter is needed, a separate feature tag should be registered and used. The RFC's example is charset, which has its own registration. The RFC notes that allowing parameters was considered and rejected because of worries about canonicalization, ordering and case sensitivity, since only exact, case-sensitive character matching is defined for media feature expressions.

The registration in Appendix A says the canonical form is the media type and subtype in lower case with all whitespace removed. Because string matching is case sensitive and whitespace sensitive, using the canonical form consistently is essential if matching is to agree with MIME content type matching.

Section 1 also says that a content type value may contain parameters but this is discouraged. Section 3 is stricter: the type must be given without them.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the file kind in one fixed way, all small letters and no spaces, so two people writing it always get exactly the same words.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows four expressions. A simple text one combines type="text/plain" with charset, color and paper-size. A fax image one uses type="image/tiff" along with tags such as dpi and image-coding.

A voice message uses type="multipart/voice-message" with tags such as audio-codec and audio-channels. Some of those features apply to MIME parts inside the multipart. The RFC says the goal is not to mirror the MIME structure but to convey useful information about the possible message content.

The last example describes a web browser. It limits screen size with pix-x<=800 and pix-y<=600, then lists alternatives joined by |: HTML with limited color, plain text, GIF with mapped color, and JPEG with full color.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are like checklists. One says 'plain text, in this alphabet, on this paper', and another says 'a fax picture, this sharp'. The browser one says 'I can show web pages, text and two kinds of pictures, on a small screen'.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content:
Appendix A asks for registration of the feature tag in the IETF tree defined in RFC 2506, which falls under the IETF Consensus policy of RFC 2434. IANA has assigned the ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.30 to the tag.

The registration says the tag indicates a MIME content type that a message agent can handle or that is contained within some message data. Its value type is String, its intended usage is Common, and the change controller is the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: The new word was written into an official list, with a number of its own, so everyone uses it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo is not believed to introduce any security considerations beyond those already inherent in using media feature tags and expressions as defined in RFC 2533 and RFC 2506.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding this one word does not open any new doors for trouble beyond what the existing system already has.
